blocks.text: Projection answers a very concrete question: if you shine a light straight down onto one vector from another, how much of that second vector actually lands on the first one. It is the operation behind finding the closest point on a line, fitting a regression line, and reducing a large dataset down to its most useful directions.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What Projection Means

Projecting vector v onto vector u means finding the point along the direction of u that sits closest to v. Picture a light shining straight down onto u from directly above v, the shadow that v casts onto the line through u is the projection.

blocks.alt: v projected straight down onto u
blocks.caption: The dashed vertical line shows how the shadow lands on u

blocks.text: The result is always a vector pointing in the exact same direction as u, since a projection can only ever stretch or shrink along the target direction, never move off to the side of it.
Projection always answers a comparison question phrased in terms of one specific direction: not how big is v overall, but how much of v points the same way as u specifically.
2. The Projection Formula

The vector projection of v onto u is computed with proj_u(v) = (dot(v, u) / dot(u, u)) * u. The fraction out front is a single scalar number, and multiplying it by u stretches or shrinks u to land exactly at the shadow point.

code.content:
import numpy as np
v = np.array([3, 4])
u = np.array([1, 0])
scale = np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)
proj = scale * u
print(proj)   # [3. 0.], v projected onto the x axis

blocks.text: The numerator, the dot product of v and u, was covered in the dot product lesson as a measure of directional overlap. Dividing it by the dot product of u with itself, which is u magnitude squared, rescales that overlap into the correct amount of u needed for the shadow.
Notice the formula never depends on the magnitude of v beyond what the dot product already captures, doubling v simply doubles the resulting projection, without changing the direction it points in.
3. Scalar Projection vs Vector Projection

There are two closely related quantities that both go by the name projection. The vector projection, covered in section 2, is an actual vector pointing along u. The scalar projection is just a single number, the signed length of that shadow, without any direction attached.

code.content:
scalar_proj = np.dot(v, u) / np.linalg.norm(u)   # a single number: signed length along u
vector_proj = (np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)) * u    # a full vector along u

blocks.content: {"headers":["Quantity","Type","Formula"],"rows":[["Scalar projection","a single number, can be negative","dot(v, u) divided by magnitude of u"],["Vector projection","a full vector along u","scalar projection times the unit vector of u"]]}

blocks.text: A negative scalar projection means v points at least partly in the opposite direction of u, the shadow still falls on the same line, just on the far side of the origin.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Projecting v = (negative 2, negative 2) onto u = (1, 0) gives a scalar projection of negative 2, signaling that v points in the opposite direction along the x axis. The vector projection in that case is (negative 2, 0), still along the line through u, just on the negative side of the origin.

blocks.text: 4. Projection in Code
The same formula from section 2 works identically regardless of how many dimensions the vectors have, which is one of the most useful properties of projection as an operation.

code.content:
v = np.array([2, 3, -1])
u = np.array([1, 1, 1])
proj = (np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)) * u
print(proj)   # [1.333 1.333 1.333]

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Projecting v = (2, 3, negative 1) onto u = (1, 1, 1) lands on (1.33, 1.33, 1.33), a point on the line through the origin in the direction (1, 1, 1). Every projection onto u, no matter which v is used, always lands somewhere on that same line.

blocks.text: This dimension-independence is what makes projection scale cleanly from simple 2D geometry examples up to feature vectors with thousands of entries used in real machine learning pipelines, the formula itself never changes.
5. Projecting onto a Unit Vector

When u is already a unit vector, as covered in the unit vector lesson, the formula from section 2 simplifies considerably, since dot(u, u) always equals 1 for a unit vector, leaving just proj_u(v) = dot(v, u) * u.

code.content:
u_hat = np.array([0, 1])          # already a unit vector
v = np.array([5, 7])
proj = np.dot(v, u_hat) * u_hat
print(proj)   # [0. 7.]

blocks.text: This is exactly why so many formulas in machine learning normalize a direction to unit length before using it, doing so removes the division step from every subsequent projection, trading a one time normalization cost for a cheaper repeated operation.

A useful habit going forward: whenever a projection direction is going to be reused many times, normalize it to a unit vector first, then every future projection onto it becomes a single dot product with no division needed.
6. Orthogonal Decomposition

Any vector v can be split into two pieces relative to a chosen direction u: the part of v lying along u, which is the projection from section 2, and the leftover part perpendicular to u. Adding those two pieces back together always reconstructs v exactly.

code.content:
proj = (np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)) * u
remainder = v - proj
print(proj + remainder)          # exactly v again
print(np.dot(remainder, u))       # 0, confirming the remainder is orthogonal to u

blocks.text: This decomposition is the geometric backbone behind splitting any signal into a wanted component and an unwanted, leftover component, a pattern that recurs throughout regression, signal processing, and dimensionality reduction alike.
6.1 Verifying the Remainder Is Perpendicular

That the remainder is always orthogonal to u is not a coincidence, it is guaranteed by construction: the projection formula is specifically designed to remove every last bit of overlap between v and u, leaving nothing but the orthogonal leftover behind, connecting directly to the dot product test from the orthogonality lesson.
7. Projection onto a Subspace

Projection generalizes beyond a single direction to an entire subspace, spanned by the columns of a matrix A. The projection matrix formula P = A (A^T A)^-1 A^T, built directly from the matrix inverse and matrix transpose lessons, projects any vector onto the closest point within the space spanned by A columns.

code.content:
A = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [0, 0]])   # spans the xy-plane inside 3D space
P = A.dot(np.linalg.inv(A.T.dot(A))).dot(A.T)
v = np.array([2, 3, 5])
print(P.dot(v))   # [2. 3. 0.], the z-component is projected away

blocks.text: This single matrix formula is the multi-dimensional generalization of the single-vector formula from section 2, and it is the mechanism behind fitting a line or plane through a cloud of points as closely as possible.

If A itself already has orthonormal columns, as covered in the orthogonality lesson, this formula simplifies considerably, since A transposed A becomes the identity matrix and the inverse step disappears entirely, leaving just P = A A transposed.
8. Projection and Least Squares Regression

Fitting a regression line means finding the combination of inputs that lands as close as possible to a set of observed target values, when an exact match is impossible. Geometrically, this is exactly a projection: the predicted values are the projection of the true target vector onto the subspace spanned by the input features, the closest point in that subspace to the actual data.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: When a regression model cannot fit every data point exactly, its best possible predictions are the projection of the true values onto the space of everything the model is capable of producing. The normal equation used to solve linear regression, mentioned in the matrix inverse lesson, is derived directly from the projection matrix formula in section 7.

blocks.text: The perpendicular remainder from section 6, in a regression setting, is exactly what statisticians call the residual, the gap between what the model predicted and what actually happened, and it is orthogonal to every input feature by the same construction covered there.
9. Projection Inside Gram-Schmidt

The orthogonality lesson introduced Gram-Schmidt as a way to build an orthogonal basis by subtracting overlap between vectors. That subtraction step is nothing other than the projection formula from section 2, applied and removed one direction at a time.

Recognizing this connection means Gram-Schmidt no longer needs to be memorized as a separate standalone algorithm, it is simply repeated projection and subtraction, applied one basis vector at a time.

Seen this way, orthogonality and projection are really two sides of the same coin: projection is the tool that measures and removes overlap, and orthogonality is simply the state where that overlap has already been reduced all the way down to zero.
10. Properties of Projection Matrices

Projection matrices built the way section 7 describes always share two properties. They are idempotent, meaning applying the projection twice gives the exact same result as applying it once, since a point already inside the subspace has nothing left to project away. They are also always symmetric, equal to their own transpose.

code.content:
P = A.dot(np.linalg.inv(A.T.dot(A))).dot(A.T)
print(np.allclose(P.dot(P), P))     # True, idempotent
print(np.allclose(P, P.T))          # True, symmetric

blocks.text: These two properties give a fast way to sanity check any matrix that is supposed to represent a projection, without needing to know what subspace it was built from in the first place.

Idempotence has a very natural real-world reading: once you have projected a dataset down onto its most important directions, projecting that already-reduced result again changes nothing further, there is no leftover overlap left to remove a second time.
11. Projection in AI Practice

items: Transformer attention layers compute query, key, and value projections by multiplying an input embedding by learned matrices, each projecting the input into a different, specialized subspace for a different purpose.

Principal component analysis, covered in the next lesson, keeps a dataset only along its most informative directions, which is exactly a projection onto the subspace spanned by the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.
Recommendation systems that use matrix factorization implicitly project a sparse ratings matrix onto a much lower dimensional space of latent user and item preferences.
Autoencoders squeeze data through a narrow bottleneck layer, forcing it through a lower dimensional subspace, and the encoding step is functionally a learned projection.

blocks.text: 12. Projection Distance and the Closest Point Property

Among every point along the direction of u, the projection is provably the single closest one to v, closer than any other scaled version of u could be. This closest-point property is the entire reason projection shows up in optimization and fitting problems: whenever a task requires finding the best possible approximation within a restricted set of options, that best approximation is a projection.

code.content:
u = np.array([1, 0])
v = np.array([3, 4])
proj = (np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)) * u   # [3, 0]
for scale in [2.5, 3, 3.5]:
    candidate = scale * u
    dist = np.linalg.norm(v - candidate)
    print(scale, dist)   # distance is smallest exactly at scale 3, matching the projection

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: Trying scale factors 2.5, 3, and 3.5 against the target v = (3, 4) shows the distance from v is smallest exactly at scale 3, which is exactly what the projection formula computes directly, without needing to search through candidate scale factors at all.

blocks.text: 13. A Worked Example
Project v = (6, 2) onto u = (3, 4) and verify the perpendicular remainder using the orthogonal decomposition from section 6.

code.content:
v = np.array([6, 2])
u = np.array([3, 4])
scale = np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)
proj = scale * u
remainder = v - proj
print(proj)                 # [3.24 4.32]
print(np.dot(remainder, u))  # close to 0

blocks.text: Double checking a projection by hand like this, comparing the computed scale factor against the raw vectors involved, is a fast habit for catching a swapped numerator and denominator before it propagates into a larger pipeline.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Dividing by dot(v, v) instead of dot(u, u) in the projection formula, the denominator always uses the vector being projected onto, not the vector being projected.
Assuming the projection always points in the same direction as v, it always points along u instead, since that is the direction being projected onto.
Forgetting the perpendicular remainder from section 6 when only the projection itself is needed, losing information that later steps, such as residual analysis in regression, often depend on.
Applying the single-vector formula from section 2 when the target is actually a subspace spanned by several vectors, which instead requires the projection matrix formula from section 7.

blocks.text: 15. Practice: Project and Decompose
Take v = (4, negative 2) and u = (1, 1). Compute the vector projection of v onto u, then compute the perpendicular remainder, and confirm the two pieces add back up to v exactly.

code.content:
v = np.array([4, -2])
u = np.array([1, 1])
proj = (np.dot(v, u) / np.dot(u, u)) * u
remainder = v - proj
print(proj, remainder, proj + remainder)

items: Computing the projection practices the core formula from section 2.
Confirming the pieces add back to v practices the orthogonal decomposition idea from section 6.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway

The closest-point property from section 12 is the deeper reason projection matters so much in applied work: whenever a problem asks for the best possible fit inside some restricted space, the mathematically optimal answer is a projection, not a guess or a search.

Projection finds how much of one vector lies along another, computed with proj_u(v) = (dot(v, u) / dot(u, u)) * u for a single direction, or with the projection matrix formula for an entire subspace. Every projection splits a vector cleanly into a piece along the target direction and a perpendicular leftover piece, which together always reconstruct the original vector exactly.

This single operation quietly underlies least squares regression, the Gram-Schmidt process from the orthogonality lesson, and the PCA and attention mechanisms covered ahead, all of which reduce, at their core, to finding the closest point within some restricted space.

The properties from section 10, idempotence and symmetry, give a quick way to confirm any matrix claimed to represent a projection actually behaves like one, a useful sanity check before trusting a larger pipeline built on top of it.
